FOIA-released 'Proximal Origin' Slack messages showed the authors of the influential paper dismissing lab leak privately considered it plausible — even as they publicly called it implausible.

questions.question: Andrew Wakefield's 1998 paper in The Lancet linking the MMR vaccine to autism was a major event in vaccine controversy. What eventually happened to the paper itself?
questions.answer: It was formally retracted by The Lancet in 2010 after fraud was documented
choices: It was formally retracted by The Lancet in 2010 after fraud was documented
It was awarded a Nobel Prize and remains the foundation of vaccine safety
It was extended into a major textbook used in medical schools worldwide
It was translated into 50 languages and remains in the journal's archive
questions.context: Wakefield's 1998 paper proposed a possible link between MMR vaccine and autism. Investigative reporter Brian Deer (Sunday Times) found that Wakefield had fabricated patient data, had undisclosed financial conflicts, and conducted unethical experiments on children. The Lancet partially retracted in 2004 and fully retracted in 2010. Wakefield lost his medical license. Many subsequent large studies have found no causal link between MMR and autism. The Wakefield episode is often cited — sometimes accurately, sometimes not — in vaccine debates; the bank covers it honestly without using slurs against critics generally.

questions.question: In September 1928 Alexander Fleming returned to his lab at St. Mary's Hospital in London after a vacation. What did he notice growing on a contaminated petri dish that changed medicine forever?
questions.answer: A mold that had killed nearby bacteria, the source of the first antibiotic
choices: A mold that had killed nearby bacteria, the source of the first antibiotic
A new species of bacteria that ate plastic from his lab equipment
A new color of bacteria never seen in laboratories before
A virus that could only grow on certain types of stained glass
questions.context: Fleming (1881-1955) noticed that a contaminating mold (later identified as Penicillium notatum) had cleared bacteria from the area around it on a petri dish. He named the active substance 'penicillin' and published in 1929 — but couldn't isolate it at useful scale. Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at Oxford did the hard chemistry in 1940-41, and Norman Heatley scaled production. By D-Day 1944 mass-produced penicillin was saving Allied soldiers. Fleming, Florey, and Chain shared the 1945 Nobel in Medicine.

questions.question: Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin's antibacterial effect in 1928 but couldn't make practical medicine from it. Who eventually isolated and produced penicillin at scale during World War II?
questions.answer: Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at Oxford University in 1940-41
choices: Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at Oxford University in 1940-41
Marie Curie's daughter Irene Joliot-Curie at the Pasteur Institute
Albert Einstein and Niels Bohr at Princeton during the war years
Robert Koch and Louis Pasteur at the German Institute of Health
questions.context: Florey (Australian pathologist) and Chain (German-Jewish chemist, refugee from Nazi Germany) led the Oxford team that isolated penicillin in usable form by 1940. Norman Heatley designed the production process. By 1941 they could treat human patients. American companies (Pfizer, Merck) scaled production to industrial levels. Florey traveled to the US to convince the wartime government to invest. By D-Day 1944, enough penicillin was available to treat every Allied soldier needing it. Fleming, Florey, and Chain shared the 1945 Nobel.

questions.question: Jonas Salk developed an effective polio vaccine using inactivated (killed) virus, tested in massive field trials in the early 1950s. What did Salk do regarding a patent for his vaccine?
questions.answer: He refused to patent it, saying it belonged to the people
choices: He refused to patent it, saying it belonged to the people
He patented it and earned billions of dollars in royalties from sales
He sold the patent to a single drug company for one dollar quietly
He patented it but the patent was rejected by the U.S. courts
questions.context: Jonas Salk (1914-1995) tested his polio vaccine on himself and his family before public trials. The 1954 field trial enrolled 1.8 million American children — the largest medical experiment ever conducted. Results announced April 12, 1955 showed the vaccine effective; church bells rang across America. When CBS journalist Edward R. Murrow asked Salk who owned the patent, Salk famously replied: 'Well, the people, I would say. There is no patent. Could you patent the sun?' Polio is now eradicated from most of the world.

questions.question: Smallpox killed roughly 300 million people in the 20th century alone. In 1980 the World Health Organization announced something that no other infectious disease has ever achieved. What?
questions.answer: Smallpox had been eradicated worldwide, no longer circulating anywhere
choices: Smallpox had been eradicated worldwide, no longer circulating anywhere
Smallpox had been renamed for political reasons in many countries
Smallpox had been moved entirely to the world's ocean reserves
Smallpox had been declared a fictional disease that never existed
questions.context: The WHO smallpox eradication program ran 1967-1980 under D.A. Henderson's leadership. The strategy was ring vaccination: identify each new case, vaccinate everyone who had been in contact, then everyone in contact with those people. The last natural case was Ali Maow Maalin in Somalia, October 1977. WHO formally declared eradication May 8, 1980 — one of humanity's greatest public-health achievements. The virus exists only in two known secured labs (CDC in Atlanta, VECTOR in Russia), kept for research.

questions.question: The very first vaccine in human history was created in 1796 by Edward Jenner, an English country doctor. What disease did he prevent, and what was the new technique called?
questions.answer: Smallpox — using cowpox material, the technique named 'vaccination' from Latin 'vacca' (cow)
choices: Smallpox — using cowpox material, the technique named 'vaccination' from Latin 'vacca' (cow)
Yellow fever — using mosquito tissue, the technique called 'mosquito-pox'
Tuberculosis — using cow's milk, the technique called 'cow-milk inoculation'
Cholera — using river water, the technique called 'aqueous immunization'
questions.context: Edward Jenner (1749-1823) noticed that milkmaids who caught the mild cowpox disease seemed protected from deadly smallpox. In 1796 he tested his hypothesis by inoculating 8-year-old James Phipps with cowpox material, then exposing him to smallpox — Phipps didn't get sick. Jenner published in 1798. The technique was called 'vaccination' from Latin 'vacca' meaning cow. Earlier 'variolation' (inoculating directly with weakened smallpox) had been practiced in Africa, India, China, and Ottoman Turkey — Lady Mary Wortley Montagu brought it to England in 1721. Jenner's safer cowpox method displaced it.

questions.question: In the 1860s French chemist Louis Pasteur showed that microorganisms cause fermentation and disease — overturning the older 'spontaneous generation' theory. What clever experimental device did he use to make his case?
questions.answer: Swan-necked flasks that let air enter but trapped airborne particles
choices: Swan-necked flasks that let air enter but trapped airborne particles
Glass tubes shaped exactly like the letter Z, viewed from above
Heated copper basins that destroyed all gases above the broth
Sealed buckets buried underground for thirty days at a time
questions.context: Pasteur's 1859 swan-neck flask experiment was elegant. He boiled broth in flasks with long, curved necks that let air in but trapped dust and microbes in the curve. The broth stayed sterile for months — no spontaneous generation. When he broke the neck, the broth was quickly contaminated. The experiment refuted spontaneous generation and supported germ theory. Pasteur went on to develop pasteurization (heat-treating to kill microbes), rabies vaccine, and improved anthrax vaccine. His work, with Robert Koch's, established germ theory.

questions.question: British surgeon Joseph Lister revolutionized surgery in the 1860s by introducing antiseptic techniques based on Pasteur's germ theory. What was his most famous antiseptic chemical?
questions.answer: Carbolic acid (phenol), used to sterilize instruments and wounds
choices: Carbolic acid (phenol), used to sterilize instruments and wounds
Hydrogen peroxide, only invented after Lister's lifetime
Bleach, the same chlorine solution used today in households
Pure alcohol, never used in medicine because of its toxicity
questions.context: Joseph Lister (1827-1912), inspired by Pasteur's germ theory, began using carbolic acid (phenol) to sterilize surgical instruments, wounds, and operating rooms in 1865 at the Glasgow Royal Infirmary. Post-surgical infection rates fell dramatically. British surgeons resisted his innovations for years (Listerism was mocked initially), but American surgeons adopted them more quickly. The mouthwash brand Listerine was named in his honor. Lister's work, together with Pasteur's, ushered in the modern era of surgical medicine.

questions.question: In November 1895 the German physicist Wilhelm Röntgen accidentally discovered a new kind of penetrating radiation in his Würzburg lab. What did he call it, and what was the first famous image he took?
questions.answer: X-rays — and the first image was of his wife's hand showing her bones
choices: X-rays — and the first image was of his wife's hand showing her bones
Y-rays — and the first image was of a fish from a nearby river
M-rays — and the first image was of a cathedral's stone walls
Z-rays — and the first image was of the Earth's underground caves
questions.context: Röntgen (1845-1923) noticed a faint glow on a fluorescent screen while working with cathode-ray tubes covered in black cardboard. Investigating further, he found an unknown form of radiation that passed through paper, wood, and flesh but not bone or metal. He called it 'X' for unknown. His December 1895 photograph of his wife Bertha's hand (showing her bones and her wedding ring) was the first medical X-ray and electrified the world. Röntgen won the very first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901 for the discovery.

questions.question: William Harvey published in 1628 that blood circulates through the body, pumped by the heart — overturning a 1500-year-old medical consensus. What was the older view he refuted?
questions.answer: That blood was made constantly by the liver and consumed by tissues
choices: That blood was made constantly by the liver and consumed by tissues
That blood was a single still puddle in the chest cavity all day
That blood was only formed when people slept at night each day
That blood was a magical substance with no physical existence at all
questions.context: The older view came from Galen (2nd century AD) and dominated Western medicine for 1500 years: the liver continuously produced new blood, which the body then consumed in tissues. William Harvey (1578-1657) calculated that the heart pumps far more blood per hour than the liver could possibly produce — therefore blood must CIRCULATE, returning to the heart. His 1628 book 'De motu cordis' (On the Motion of the Heart) overturned Galenic medicine. Harvey's work shows that long-held consensus can be wrong, and that careful measurement can defeat ancient authority.

questions.question: Antoine Lavoisier (1743-1794) overturned the old 'phlogiston theory' of burning by identifying the actual chemistry of combustion. What did Lavoisier name the gas that combines with burning materials?
questions.answer: Oxygen, from Greek for 'acid-former'
choices: Oxygen, from Greek for 'acid-former'
Phlogiston, keeping the old chemical name as an honor
Nitrogen, mistakenly using a name later assigned to a different gas
Helium, naming it after the Sun for its bright flames
questions.context: Phlogiston theory held that burning materials released a substance called 'phlogiston.' Lavoisier (in the 1770s-80s) showed that burning materials COMBINE with a gas (oxygen) from air, GAINING mass. He named oxygen from Greek 'oxys' (sharp/acid) + 'genes' (former) because he believed it formed all acids (a partial misunderstanding). Lavoisier also identified hydrogen, established the law of conservation of mass, and built modern chemical nomenclature. He was guillotined in 1794 during the French Revolution at age 50. The mathematician Lagrange said: 'It took only a moment to cause that head to fall, and a hundred years will not be sufficient to produce another like it.'

questions.question: Dmitri Mendeleev published his periodic table in 1869, arranging the known chemical elements by atomic weight in rows and columns. What striking feature of his table convinced chemists it was correct?
questions.answer: Gaps that predicted undiscovered elements, all of which were later found
choices: Gaps that predicted undiscovered elements, all of which were later found
An exact alphabetical arrangement of every element by English name
Color-coded illustrations that made it easy for children to memorize
A list ordered by which element was most abundant on Earth's surface
questions.context: Mendeleev (1834-1907) arranged elements by atomic weight and noticed periodic recurrences of chemical properties. To preserve the pattern, he left gaps for predicted-but-unknown elements — including specific predictions of their atomic weights, densities, and reactivity. Gallium (1875), scandium (1879), and germanium (1886) were all later discovered matching Mendeleev's predictions closely. The successful predictions convinced even skeptical chemists. Modern periodic tables order elements by atomic NUMBER (protons), not atomic weight — but Mendeleev's organizational insight remains intact.

questions.question: Wegener was rejected for 50 years over continental drift; Semmelweis was institutionalized for showing hand-washing saves lives; Marshall was ridiculed over the H. pylori-ulcer link. What lesson do these cases teach?
questions.answer: Scientific consensus has been wrong many times and can update
choices: Scientific consensus has been wrong many times and can update
Scientific consensus has always been right and never changes
Outsiders to science are always wrong about medical claims
Scientific debates are decided only by public votes citywide
questions.context: Wegener (continental drift, 1912 rejected, 1960s vindicated), Semmelweis (hand-washing, 1847 mocked, posthumously vindicated), Marshall + Warren (H. pylori, 1980s ridiculed, 2005 Nobel) are three classic cases — and there are more (Lister antisepsis, Mendel ignored, plate tectonics). The pattern doesn't mean every fringe claim is right (most are wrong). It does mean appealing to consensus as the final answer is bad epistemology. Real science updates; the careful question isn't 'do experts agree?' but 'what does the evidence actually show?'

questions.question: Beginning around 2010, several large research efforts tried to replicate famous findings in psychology and biomedicine. What did these efforts often find?
questions.answer: Many famous results failed to replicate when independent labs tried again
choices: Many famous results failed to replicate when independent labs tried again
Every famous result was perfectly replicated by every other lab
Famous results are impossible to replicate by definition of being unique
Famous results were all classified secret and could not be retested
questions.context: The 'replication crisis' is the recognition that many published findings — especially in social psychology, but also in cancer biology and pharmacology — don't replicate when independent labs try them. The 2015 Open Science Collaboration replication of 100 psychology studies found only ~36% replicated cleanly. Famous failed replications include ego depletion, power-pose effect, priming effects. Causes include p-hacking, publication bias (positive results get published, null results don't), small sample sizes, and outright fraud (Diederik Stapel, ~50 retractions). The crisis has led to pre-registration, larger studies, and more cautious interpretation of single studies.

questions.question: In 2005 epidemiologist John Ioannidis published a famous paper applying Bayesian reasoning to scientific publishing. What was the title and key claim?
questions.answer: 'Why Most Published Research Findings Are False' — single studies are weak evidence
choices: 'Why Most Published Research Findings Are False' — single studies are weak evidence
'Why Every Scientific Paper Is Always Correct' — papers should be trusted absolutely
'Why Scientists Should Stop Publishing' — research should remain unpublished forever
'Why Public Funding Always Fails' — only private grants produce valid science
questions.context: John Ioannidis (Stanford epidemiologist, born 1965) published 'Why Most Published Research Findings Are False' in PLOS Medicine in August 2005. He applied Bayesian reasoning about prior probabilities, study power, bias, and competition to show that — given typical practices — most published findings should be expected to be false. The paper has been cited tens of thousands of times. Ioannidis became one of the leading voices in the replication-crisis discussion, and was a notable Great Barrington Declaration signatory critical of pandemic lockdown policies.

questions.question: In 1887 Albert Michelson and Edward Morley conducted a famous experiment trying to detect Earth's motion through a supposed medium called the 'luminiferous ether.' What did they find?
questions.answer: No detectable motion through any ether, since the ether didn't exist
choices: No detectable motion through any ether, since the ether didn't exist
Earth moving at exactly the predicted speed through the ether
An ether wind so strong it nearly destroyed the apparatus
Multiple ethers each moving in different directions at the time
questions.context: Michelson and Morley used a sensitive interferometer to compare light speeds in different directions. If Earth was moving through an ether, light should travel faster downstream than across. They found no difference at all — a 'null result.' The puzzle stood for nearly 20 years until Einstein's 1905 special relativity explained why: there is no ether, and the speed of light is the same for all observers regardless of motion. The Michelson-Morley experiment is one of the most famous 'beautiful failures' in physics — the failure itself was the discovery.

questions.question: Einstein's 1915 general relativity predicted gravity would bend starlight near the Sun. The 1919 total solar eclipse offered the first major test. Who led the confirming expedition?
questions.answer: Arthur Eddington, who photographed stars near the eclipsed Sun from Príncipe
choices: Arthur Eddington, who photographed stars near the eclipsed Sun from Príncipe
Edwin Hubble, observing only from Mount Wilson in California
Albert Michelson, attempting another null result like 1887
Marie Curie, joining the expedition from Paris during the war
questions.context: Arthur Eddington (1882-1944), a British astronomer and Quaker pacifist, led an expedition to the island of Príncipe (off West Africa) to photograph the total solar eclipse of May 29, 1919. A parallel expedition went to Sobral, Brazil. The photographs showed star positions shifted by about Einstein's predicted amount, vindicating general relativity over Newton. The November 1919 announcement made Einstein a global celebrity overnight. Modern reanalysis has questioned how confidently the 1919 data alone could distinguish the theories — but later confirmations are airtight.

questions.question: Robert Millikan won the 1923 Nobel Prize in Physics for measuring the electric charge of a single electron. What experimental technique did he use?
questions.answer: Watching tiny oil droplets fall and rise between charged plates
choices: Watching tiny oil droplets fall and rise between charged plates
Counting raindrops on a London window during one rainy day
Throwing magnets in the air to attract electrons from clouds
Heating water until electrons appeared in the steam visibly
questions.context: Millikan's 1909 oil-drop experiment used an atomizer to spray microscopic oil droplets between two horizontal metal plates. By measuring how fast individual droplets fell under gravity and then adjusting the plate voltage to slow or reverse their fall, he calculated the charge on each droplet. He found all measured charges were integer multiples of a fundamental unit — the electron's charge, 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ coulombs. Subsequent reviews of Millikan's notebooks suggest he may have selectively reported data, but the measured value held up to later precise determinations.

questions.question: Thomas Young's 1801 double-slit experiment provided strong evidence about the nature of light. What surprising result did he find?
questions.answer: Light created interference patterns, behaving as a wave and not just particles
choices: Light created interference patterns, behaving as a wave and not just particles
Light disappeared entirely when passing through any two narrow slits
Light split into rainbow colors only at certain seasons of the year
Light only worked when shone through perfectly square openings
questions.context: Young (1773-1829) shone light through two close-spaced parallel slits onto a screen. Instead of two bright spots (as expected if light was particles), he saw an interference pattern with alternating bright and dark bands — exactly what happens when waves overlap. His experiment overturned Newton's earlier 'corpuscular' theory of light as particles. In the 20th century, the same double-slit experiment performed with single electrons produced the same wave pattern — one of the strangest results in quantum physics. Light is both wave AND particle, depending on what you measure.

questions.question: Johannes Kepler (1571-1630) published the rules that planets follow as they orbit the Sun. What was his most counter-intuitive finding about planetary orbits?
questions.answer: Planets orbit in ellipses, not circles as believed for 2000 years
choices: Planets orbit in ellipses, not circles as believed for 2000 years
Planets orbit only on Tuesdays and stop at all other times
Planets are perfectly stationary and the Sun moves around them
Planets all orbit at the exact same speed regardless of their size
questions.context: Kepler used Tycho Brahe's precise observations of Mars to discover that planets follow elliptical (oval) orbits with the Sun at one focus. This overturned the ancient Greek-and-medieval assumption that celestial bodies must move in perfect circles. Kepler's three laws (1609, 1619) became the empirical foundation Newton used to derive universal gravitation in 1687. Kepler also discovered that planets sweep out equal areas in equal times (faster when closer to the Sun) and that orbital period squared is proportional to semi-major axis cubed.

questions.question: In 1909-1911 Ernest Rutherford and his students at Manchester directed alpha particles at thin gold foil. What surprising result reshaped the atomic model?
questions.answer: A few particles bounced almost straight back, so atoms must have tiny dense nuclei
choices: A few particles bounced almost straight back, so atoms must have tiny dense nuclei
Every single particle passed straight through, suggesting atoms are entirely empty
Every particle stopped immediately, suggesting atoms are entirely solid all through
The gold foil ignited and burned brightly, confirming no atomic structure exists
questions.context: Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden, working in Rutherford's lab, observed that ~1 in 8000 alpha particles bounced backward — like a 15-inch shell bouncing off tissue paper. Rutherford's interpretation (1911): atoms aren't uniform 'plum puddings' (J.J. Thomson's earlier model). Almost all the mass is concentrated in a tiny dense nucleus at the center, with electrons orbiting at distance. This model was refined by Bohr (1913) and finally absorbed into quantum mechanics in the 1920s.

questions.question: Dmitri Mendeleev's periodic table grouped elements with similar chemical behavior in the same column. What did this organization eventually reveal about the underlying structure of atoms?
questions.answer: Elements in the same column have similar outer-electron configurations
choices: Elements in the same column have similar outer-electron configurations
Elements in the same column are all liquids at room temperature
Elements in the same column all have exactly the same atomic weight
Elements in the same column come from the same star originally
questions.context: Mendeleev grouped elements by chemical behavior in 1869 without knowing about electrons or atomic structure. We now know that elements in the same column share outer-electron (valence shell) configurations — which determines their chemistry. The noble gases (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn) all have full outer shells, making them chemically inert. The halogens (F, Cl, Br, I) all lack one electron, making them highly reactive. Atomic structure (Bohr 1913, Schrödinger 1926) eventually explained why Mendeleev's empirical pattern existed.

questions.question: Before the 1860s most diseases were thought to be caused by 'miasma' (bad air) or imbalanced humors. Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch overturned this view. What did they show diseases are actually caused by?
questions.answer: Specific microorganisms, bacteria and other microbes invisible to the eye
choices: Specific microorganisms, bacteria and other microbes invisible to the eye
Bad luck and individual moral failings that cannot be measured
Curses placed on specific families by other people deliberately
Old age alone, with no other identifiable causes whatsoever
questions.context: Germ theory developed through the work of many — Ignaz Semmelweis (hand-washing, 1847), Louis Pasteur (microbes cause fermentation and disease, 1860s), Joseph Lister (antiseptic surgery, 1860s), and Robert Koch (proving specific microbes cause specific diseases: anthrax 1876, tuberculosis 1882, cholera 1884). Koch's postulates established how to prove a particular microbe caused a particular disease. The germ theory transformed medicine: by 1900 once-deadly diseases (puerperal fever, surgical infection, cholera) had been substantially reduced where germ-theory hygiene was adopted.

questions.question: James Watson's 1968 memoir 'The Double Helix' offered an unusually frank — and controversial — account of the DNA-structure discovery. What was particularly controversial about the book?
questions.answer: Its dismissive treatment of Rosalind Franklin, criticized as ungenerous and sexist
choices: Its dismissive treatment of Rosalind Franklin, criticized as ungenerous and sexist
Its claim that Watson had personally discovered every step alone
Its claim that the structure was wrong and should be re-derived
Its claim that Crick had not actually been involved in any way
questions.context: Watson's 'The Double Helix' (1968) was praised for its candor about the messiness of real science but harshly criticized for its treatment of Rosalind Franklin. Watson described her as obstructive and intellectually limited, with frequent comments on her appearance and clothing. Crick and others pushed back. Aaron Klug (Franklin's colleague) and Anne Sayre's biography 'Rosalind Franklin and DNA' (1975) corrected the record. Watson himself later expressed some regret over the framing. Subsequent histories give Franklin substantial credit for the structural insights, though Nobel rules excluded her posthumously.

questions.question: After the Permian-Triassic 'Great Dying' extinction wiped out ~90% of marine species, how long did Earth's biosphere take to recover its previous diversity?
questions.answer: About 10 million years, with marine reefs gone the whole time
choices: About 10 million years, with marine reefs gone the whole time
About 100 years, with recovery complete by the next century
About 1,000 years, completing in a single millennium
About 1 billion years, with recovery still ongoing today
questions.context: The Permian-Triassic extinction (252 million years ago) so devastated Earth's ecosystems that recovery took roughly 10 million years. Marine reefs essentially disappeared and didn't reform for 10 million years. On land, the 'coal gap' of the early Triassic shows almost no plant deposits — forests took as long to recover. The new biota that emerged was dominated by archosaurs (eventually leading to dinosaurs and modern crocodilians). The Great Dying reshaped which lineages would dominate Earth for the next ~180 million years.

questions.question: In 1925 a young Tennessee high school teacher named John Scopes was put on trial for teaching evolution, violating the state's recent Butler Act. What was the outcome of the trial?
questions.answer: Scopes was convicted and fined $100, with the verdict later overturned on a technicality
choices: Scopes was convicted and fined $100, with the verdict later overturned on a technicality
Scopes was acquitted unanimously by the jury after one day of testimony
Scopes won a million dollars in damages from the State of Tennessee
Scopes died during the trial and the proceedings were canceled outright
questions.context: John Scopes (1900-1970) was a substitute teacher who agreed to be the test case after the ACLU offered to defend any teacher charged under Tennessee's 1925 Butler Act (banning teaching of evolution in public schools). Clarence Darrow defended Scopes; William Jennings Bryan led the prosecution. The trial became a national spectacle. Scopes was convicted and fined $100. The Tennessee Supreme Court overturned on a technicality (the fine had been set by judge not jury). The Butler Act remained on Tennessee books until 1967.

questions.question: The 'Big Bang' theory of cosmic origins was first proposed in 1927 by a scientist who was also a Catholic priest. Who was he, and what did he call his original idea?
questions.answer: Georges Lemaître, who called it the 'primeval atom' hypothesis
choices: Georges Lemaître, who called it the 'primeval atom' hypothesis
Edwin Hubble, calling it the 'expanding universe' idea
Albert Einstein, calling it the 'cosmological constant' problem
Gregor Mendel, calling it the 'inheritance of cosmic matter' theory
questions.context: Father Georges Lemaître (1894-1966), Belgian priest and physicist, proposed in 1927 that the universe began as a single 'primeval atom' that expanded outward. The idea was initially controversial (some accused him of importing Genesis into physics). Edwin Hubble's 1929 observations of galaxy redshifts supported expansion. The name 'Big Bang' was coined sarcastically by Fred Hoyle in 1949 — Hoyle preferred the rival 'Steady State' theory. Pope Pius XII embraced the Big Bang in 1951; Lemaître asked the Pope to stop, arguing science and theology should stay separate.

questions.question: Tycho Brahe (1546-1601), a Danish nobleman, built the most accurate naked-eye astronomical observatory in history at Uraniborg on the island of Hven. Why did his observations turn out to be so important?
questions.answer: They were precise enough for Kepler to derive the laws of planetary motion
choices: They were precise enough for Kepler to derive the laws of planetary motion
They proved the Earth-centered model of the universe definitively
They predicted the exact date of every solar eclipse for the next thousand years
They discovered the existence of all eight planets of our solar system
questions.context: Tycho Brahe's observations of planetary positions were accurate to about 1 arcminute — astonishing for naked-eye instruments. He had a famously colorful life: a metal nose (lost in a youthful duel), a pet elk that died after drinking too much beer, and a private island given to him by the Danish king. After his death (1601), his assistant Johannes Kepler inherited his data. Kepler's analysis of Tycho's Mars observations led to the discovery that planets follow elliptical orbits — the foundation Newton would build on.

questions.question: When Joseph Lister introduced antiseptic surgery using carbolic acid in 1865, British surgeons resisted his techniques for years. What links this resistance to other cases like Semmelweis and Wegener?
questions.answer: Established practitioners often resist methods that challenge their training
choices: Established practitioners often resist methods that challenge their training
British surgeons accepted Lister's methods immediately and unanimously
Lister abandoned his methods after British surgeons rejected them all
Lister's methods were endorsed by Parliament before any clinical trial
questions.context: Lister published his results in 1867 in The Lancet — post-surgical infection rates dropped dramatically using carbolic acid. British surgeons were skeptical (Lister was Scottish and at Glasgow, not the London establishment); they doubted germ theory and were proud of their existing techniques (the 'good old surgical stink' was sometimes worn as a badge of honor). American surgeons adopted Listerism more quickly. The Semmelweis-Lister-Marshall pattern shows that mid-career practitioners can be the most resistant to evidence — a recurring obstacle in medical reform.

questions.question: Historians sometimes use the term 'Scientific Revolution' for a roughly two-century period when modern science emerged. What dates do most historians bracket the Scientific Revolution between?
questions.answer: Roughly 1543 (Copernicus) to 1687 (Newton's Principia)
choices: Roughly 1543 (Copernicus) to 1687 (Newton's Principia)
Roughly 1066 (Norman Conquest) to 1500 (early Renaissance only)
Roughly 1800 (Industrial Revolution) to 2000 (modern science only)
Roughly 700 BC (Greek philosophy) to 1500 AD (Renaissance start)
questions.context: The 'Scientific Revolution' is conventionally bracketed by Copernicus's 'On the Revolutions' (1543) and Newton's 'Principia' (1687). Major moments: Copernicus's heliocentrism (1543); Vesalius's anatomy (1543); Galileo's telescope (1609) and trial (1633); Kepler's laws (1609, 1619); Harvey on blood circulation (1628); Royal Society founded (1660); Newton's optics (1672) and Principia (1687). The period saw the emergence of experimental method, mathematical natural philosophy, and the institutions (academies, journals, peer review) that we still use today.

questions.question: One of the world's oldest scientific societies was founded in London in 1660 and still operates today. What is it called?
questions.answer: The Royal Society of London for Improving Natural Knowledge
choices: The Royal Society of London for Improving Natural Knowledge
The American Academy of Sciences, founded that year by colonists
The Vatican Pontifical Academy, founded in the year 1666 in Rome
The Russian Academy, founded by Peter the Great in St. Petersburg
questions.context: The Royal Society was founded November 28, 1660 by 12 men who included Robert Boyle, Christopher Wren, and John Wilkins. King Charles II granted a royal charter in 1662. The society's motto 'Nullius in verba' ('take no one's word for it') captures its founding spirit: empirical evidence, not appeal to authority. Members have included Newton, Darwin, Maxwell, Rutherford, Curie, Einstein, Crick, Watson, and Hawking. The Society's 'Philosophical Transactions' (founded 1665) is one of the longest-running scientific journals in the world.

questions.question: Trofim Lysenko was a Soviet agronomist who dominated Russian biology from the 1930s through 1965. The Soviet state backed his ideas while suppressing real genetics. What is the broader lesson of his career?
questions.answer: Politically-favored science can suppress real biology for decades
choices: Politically-favored science can suppress real biology for decades
Politically-favored science always agrees with real biology
Lysenko was correct and Western biology is still wrong on genes
The Soviet government had no influence on which ideas prevailed
questions.context: Trofim Lysenko (1898-1976) rejected Mendelian genetics in favor of a Lamarckian view that organisms could pass on acquired traits. Stalin and Khrushchev backed him; geneticists who disagreed were dismissed, imprisoned, or executed (Nikolai Vavilov, the great seed-bank founder, died in prison in 1943). Soviet agriculture suffered famines partly from Lysenko's failed crop programs. Lysenkoism dominated until 1965. The episode is the clearest 20th-century case of political ideology imposed onto biology — and a warning about the cost of suppressing scientific dissent.
